html:
Monitors and condition triggers

A monitor checks command output on one Gateway for a condition. It records observations and can create a notification and an Agent action when the condition matches. Use Schedules for work that should happen at a future time. A monitor needs an actual command and a finite duration; describing a desired outcome alone does not establish how to observe it.

Each monitor captures one Gateway and its accepted execution context. Structured selections containing sibling Gateways are rejected. A triggered Agent task retains that single-Gateway scope. Its progress and result are separate from the monitor's own status: triggered means the condition matched and trigger handling ran, not that the resulting action succeeded.

For worker ownership and execution sequences, see Monitor workers and trigger flow.

Create and inspect a monitor

The native monitor.start tool requires an explicit command. Supply the condition, mode, interval and duration deliberately, then retain the returned monitor_id. monitor.inspect and monitor.stop use observed IDs. The native start adapter does not call a drafting model to fill in a missing command.

The explicit draft/create HTTP workflow can turn a prompt into proposed settings. It recognizes a monitor request, optionally asks the configured drafting model, validates its response and falls back to local rules when the proposal is unavailable or invalid. A backticked command takes the deterministic path. Known memory, GPU and disk probes may still be rewritten into more parseable forms during validation; inspect the resulting command before starting it. An incomplete draft has missing details and is not ready to run.

Creation defaults to sampling every 5 seconds for 300 seconds. Manager-owned creation clamps duration to the configured maximum, which defaults to 300 seconds, including an explicitly supplied duration. Review the returned definition to see the accepted values. The command checks reject known destructive patterns and unsupported interactive programs; they are heuristic checks, not a complete shell parser or an independent authorization boundary.

Mode Observations Timing behavior
sample_command Runs the command, collects stdout/stderr and exit status, then records one sample. Checks duration between commands and waits the configured interval between samples. A slow command can exceed the requested duration.
raw_stream Runs one command and evaluates arriving output events separately. Checks cancellation/duration when an event arrives. A silent stream can delay those checks; conditions do not combine text across chunks.

Known watch and tail -f forms select streaming during creation validation. The monitor manager opens its own terminal on the chosen Gateway; its command output is observation data and does not itself authorize further actions.

Conditions and model judgement

Condition Meaning
contains:ready Case-insensitive substring match.
regex:... Python regular expression with case-insensitive and multiline matching. Invalid syntax can fail the worker.
number_lt:2048 / number_gt:90 Compare the first numeric token in the output with the threshold. Put the relevant metric first; this does not select a named column or inspect every value.
exit_code_nonzero Match a supplied nonzero exit status.
Plain text Case-insensitive substring fallback. An empty condition does not match.

deterministic evaluates these rules without model calls. llm_judged uses a natural-language condition and the configured judge. hybrid tries the deterministic condition first and asks the judge only when it did not match. A model trigger requires both should_trigger=true and confidence of at least 0.5.

The judge uses the larger of the monitor cadence and the configured minimum (default 5 seconds). It receives bounded output, not the full command history. If the provider is unavailable, its result is invalid, or the inference budget is exhausted, the monitor records a judge diagnostic and continues collecting observations. Native model-led monitors reserve each call against a stored lifetime allowance, default 32; a failed call still consumes its reserved slot. Restarting the process does not reset that stored count.

Judge-proposed action context is stored under monitor_judge_task_context; it does not replace the monitor's captured authority. An action task is created only when an action prompt and task service exist. Notifications are handled by the existing Notification Center store and delivery settings.

Lifecycle, edits and recovery

Pause and cancel signal the local worker and request Gateway cancellation when an execution ID is available. The request is best effort: the returned status does not prove that the remote process has ended. Wait for the worker to settle before editing or deleting its definition. Starting an existing running monitor reuses its worker; starting a stopped monitor begins another worker with the saved settings and retained history.

Definition edits and deletion require the exact observed updated_at revision. The native monitor.update and monitor.delete operations use the same Controller routes and revision checks as HTTP management. A stale revision, open status or live worker produces a conflict; read the monitor again before deciding what to change. Edits accept named definition fields and retain captured context. They do not restart execution or rerun the full creation/drafting normalization. Inspect changed commands and timing explicitly.

Archiving hides a monitor and retains its history. Deletion removes the stopped monitor and its observations/triggers; already created tasks and notifications remain independent. On Controller restart, visible queued, running and paused records are marked interrupted, with their prior error reason retained when present. Recovery does not automatically restart their remote commands.

The active Controller keeps monitor state in the shared RAM authority and saves it through Controller state and recovery. Standalone stores use SQLite. Observation insertion and the latest-observation pointer are one transaction in either adapter. Trigger handling crosses several operations—task creation, monitor state, notification, trigger receipt—so a later failure can leave earlier effects recorded. Read those linked records when diagnosing partial work.

History and troubleshooting

Observations are paged in ascending sequence order, using after_sequence as an exclusive cursor; a page contains at most 1,000 records. The latest observation is also available by its stored ID. Trigger history is newest first. Stored stdout and stderr retain 12,000-character prefixes, and previews retain 4,000 characters, with an additional truncation marker when needed. These are clipped records, not full terminal transcripts.

Several internal helpers currently use bounded ascending history prefixes. The judge combines the first eight stored observations with the current output and keeps a bounded tail. Completion summaries use the last item of a five-record prefix. Sequence allocation reads the first 1,000 observations, so longer histories can reuse sequence values and make cursor-based views incomplete. Use the stored latest-observation reference when inspecting recent evidence; do not treat the summary or judge input as proof that every sample was examined.

Creation-time retention defaults to 5,000 settled monitors while preserving queued, running and paused records. RAM pruning removes their child histories too. The standalone SQL retention statement only explicitly removes monitor rows; explicit definition deletion removes children in both adapters. Output and context records are not independently redacted merely by being serialized. Keep credentials out of commands and recorded context, and use normal access controls for inspection.

Symptom What to inspect
No trigger despite an apparent numeric threshold Check the first numeric token and whether the current event contains the complete signal.
Judge unavailable or no judged trigger Read latest_judge_summary, observation detail, cadence, confidence and remaining lifetime allowance.
Cancelled status with remote activity Inspect the Gateway execution/terminal; cancellation does not synchronously join the worker or prove remote termination.
Edit/delete conflict Refresh updated_at, confirm stopped status and wait for the worker to settle.
Interrupted after restart Review the retained record and decide whether another run is appropriate.
Trigger exists but action did not finish Follow the recorded task and notification IDs; inspect partial trigger effects and the task's own outcome.

Configuration and implementation

The Controller reads these defaults from its settings definitions. Normal startup configuration loading still applies; changing an environment variable does not retroactively change an existing manager or saved monitor.

Environment variable Default Effect
AOR_MONITOR_DRAFTING_ENABLED true Enables the optional model drafter in the explicit draft workflow; local rules remain available.
AOR_LLM_TRIGGER_JUDGE_ENABLED true Enables configured natural-language/hybrid condition judgement.
AOR_MONITOR_JUDGE_MIN_INTERVAL_SECONDS 5 Global minimum judge cadence, normalized to at least one second.
AOR_MONITOR_JUDGE_OUTPUT_PREVIEW_CAP 4000 Character cap for the judge input tail, normalized to at least 500.
AOR_MAX_INFERRED_MONITOR_DURATION_SECONDS 300 Maximum duration applied by draft and manager creation validation.
flowchart TD D[Explicit draft workflow] --> V[Validate monitor settings] N[Native tool with explicit command] --> V V --> S[Monitor definition store] S --> M[Manager worker and cancellation handles] M --> G[One Gateway terminal] G --> O[Command or stream observation] O --> C[Deterministic condition] O --> J[Optional bounded model judge] C --> E[Stored observation and match evidence] J --> E E --> T[Trigger handling] T --> A[Independent Agent action task] T --> I[Notification and trigger receipt]

The monitor source folder identifies each implementation owner. HTTP routes expose create/draft, inspection, SSE and lifecycle operations; service wiring supplies Gateway, task and model providers. Settings define configuration defaults, and native adapters enforce the explicit-command entry point. Focused examples are covered by RAM monitor tests, drafting and judge fixtures, and native lifecycle/budget cases.
